L100: L101: Copy page Copy page L102: ## What is authorization? L103: L104: Authorization is the process of granting a connection or token access to Notion data. 【39†Internal connections】 use a static credential called an internal connection API token, 【40†personal access tokens】 use a user-scoped static token, and 【41†OAuth integrations】 and 【42†public integrations】 use the 【43†OAuth 2.0†oauth.net】 protocol. L105: ## Internal connection auth flow set-up L106: L107: To use an internal connection, start by creating your connection in the 【44†Developer portal†app.notion.com】. The internal connection will be associated with the workspace of your choice. You are required to be a workspace owner to create a connection. L108: L109: 【45†Image: The integrations list includes a New integration button.†mintcdn.com】 L110: L111: Create a new connection from the Developer portal. L112: Once the connection is created, you can update its settings as needed under the `Configuration` tab and retrieve the API token in this tab. The API token will be used to authenticate REST API requests. The connection sends the same token in every API request. L113: L114: 【46†Image: The internal integration settings show a masked token with a Show button.†mintcdn.com】 L115: L116: Find the API token in the Configuration tab. L117: ### Connection permissions L118: Before a connection can interact with your Notion workspace page(s), the page must be manually shared with the connection. To share a page with a connection, visit the page in your Notion workspace, click the ••• menu at the top right of a page, scroll down to `Add connections`, and use the search bar to find and select the connection from the dropdown list. Once the connection is shared, you can start making API requests. If the page is not shared, any API requests made will respond with an error. L119: Never share your API token Your API token is a secret. To keep your connection secure, never store the token in your source code or commit it in version control. Instead, read the token from an environment variable. Use a secret manager or deployment system to set the token in the environment.【10†Learn more: Best Practices for Handling API Keys】 L120: ### Making API requests with an internal connection L121: L122: Any time your connection interacts with your workspace, include the API token in the `Authorization` header with every API request. However, if you are using Notion’s 【47†SDK for JavaScript†github.com】 to interact with the REST API, the token is set once when a client is initialized. L123: L124: HTTP L125: L126: `GET /v1/pages/b55c9c91-384d-452b-81db-d1ef79372b75 HTTP/1.1 L127: Authorization: Bearer {INTEGRATION_TOKEN} L128: ` L129: JavaScript L130: L131: `const { Client } = require("@notionhq/client") L132: L133: // Initializing a client L134: const notion = new Client({ L135: auth: process.env.NOTION_TOKEN, L136: }) L137: L138: const getUsers = async () => { L139: const listUsersResponse = await notion.users.list({}) L140: } L141: ` L142: L143: If you are not using the 【47†Notion SDK for JavaScript†github.com】, also set the 【48†`Notion-Version`】 and 【49†`Content-type`†developer.mozilla.org】 headers in all of your requests, like so: L144: JSON L145: L146: `headers: { L147: Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.NOTION_TOKEN}`, L148: "Notion-Version": "2026-03-11", L149: "Content-Type": "application/json", L150: }, L151: ` L152: L153: If you receive an error response from the API, check if the connection has been properly 【50†added to the page†www.notion.com】. If this does not solve the problem, refer to our 【51†Status codes】 page for more information. L154: ## Personal access token authentication L155: Personal access tokens (PATs) are created directly by a Notion user in the 【52†Developer portal†www.notion.so】. There is no OAuth flow and no page picker. A PAT acts as the user who created it and uses that user’s permissions in the selected workspace. Use a PAT when a script, CLI workflow, Worker, or trusted tool should act as you. Use an internal connection for team-owned workspace automations, or an OAuth integration when each user needs to authorize your app. L156: PATs use the same `Authorization` header as other credentials for the Notion API: L157: HTTP L158: L159: `GET /v1/users/me HTTP/1.1 L160: Authorization: Bearer {PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN} L161: Notion-Version: 2026-03-11 L162: ` L163: L164: See 【40†Personal access tokens】 for creation steps, workspace admin controls, tier defaults, and security guidance. L165: ## OAuth integration auth flow set-up L166: L167: An OAuth integration can be installed in any Notion workspace within its 【53†installation scope】 — a specific set chosen at creation time for scoped integrations, or any workspace for public integrations. An OAuth integration isn’t tied to a single workspace through an internal connection API token. Instead, OAuth integrations follow the 【43†OAuth 2.0 protocol†oauth.net】 to authorize a connection to interact with a workspace. L168: ### How to make an OAuth integration L169: Navigate to the 【44†Developer portal†app.notion.com】 and create a new OAuth integration. Fill out the form with your connection details, including your redirect URI(s) under the OAuth configuration section and the connection’s 【53†installation scope】 — either Any workspace or Or select 1 or more workspaces. This can’t be changed after creation. The redirect URI is the URI your users will be redirected to after authorizing the OAuth integration. L170: To learn more, read 【54†OAuth’s description of redirect URIs†www.oauth.com】. L171: Marketplace listing details (such as descriptions, categories, and images) are managed separately through the Listings section. Refer to the 【55†List on the Marketplace】 guide to learn more. L172: ### OAuth integration authorization overview L173: L174: Both scoped OAuth integrations and public integrations use this flow. You can start authorization as soon as you configure the integration’s client credentials and redirect URI; Marketplace submission or review is not required. As an overview, the authorization flow includes the following steps. Each step will be described in more detail below. L175: L176: 1 L177: Navigate the user to the connection’s authorization URL. This URL is provided in the 【44†Developer portal†app.notion.com】. L178: L179: 2 L180: L181: After the user selects which workspace pages to share, Notion redirects the user to the connection’s redirect URI and includes a `code` query parameter. The redirect URI is the one you specified in your 【44†Developer portal†app.notion.com】. L182: L183: 3 L184: L185: Make a `POST` request to 【56†create an access token】, which exchanges the temporary `code` for an access token. L186: L187: 4 L188: The Notion API responds with an access token and some additional information. L189: L190: 5 L191: L192: Store the access token for future API requests. View the 【4†API reference docs】 to learn about available endpoints. L193: ### Step 1 - Navigate the user to the connection’s authorization URL L194: L195: After creating an OAuth integration in the 【44†Developer portal†app.notion.com】, access the connection’s secrets in the Configuration tab. Similarly to the internal connections, these values should be protected and should never be included in source code or version control. L196: L197: 【57†Image: The OAuth integration settings show a URL to start authorization.†mintcdn.com】 L198: The Configuration tab provides the authorization URL for your OAuth integration L199: L200: As an example, your `.env` file using these secrets could look like this: L201: L202: Shell L203: L204: `#.env L205: L206: OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= L207: OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= L208: NOTION_AUTH_URL= L209: ` L210: To start the authorization flow for an OAuth integration, direct the prospective user to the authorization URL. A common pattern is to include a hyperlink in the connection app that interacts with the Notion REST API. For example, an app that lets users create Notion pages in their workspaces should send users to the authorization URL first. The following example shows an authorization URL made available through a hyperlink: L211: HTML L212: L213: `Add to Notion L214: ` L215: L216: The URL begins with `https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/authorize` and has the following parameters: L217: Parameter | Description | Required L218: --- | --- | --- L219: `client_id` | An identifier for your connection, found in the connection settings. | ✅ L220: `redirect_uri` | The URL where the user should return after granting access. | ✅ L221: `response_type` | Always use `code`. | ✅ L222: `owner` | Always use `user`. | ✅ L223: `state` | If the user was in the middle of an interaction or operation, then this parameter can be used to restore state after the user returns. It can also be used to prevent CSRF attacks. | L224: Once the authorization URL is visited, the user will be shown a prompt that varies depending on whether or not the connection comes with a Notion template option. L225: #### Prompt for a standard connection with no template option (Default) L226: L227: In the standard connection permissions flow, a prompt describes the connection 【58†capabilities】, presented to the user as what the connection would like to be able to do in the workspace. A user can either select pages to grant the connection access to, or cancel the request. L228: L229: 【59†Image: The authorization prompt lists what the connection can do before the user selects pages.†mintcdn.com】 L230: Prompt for authorizing a standard connection (no template option) L231: L232: If the user presses Cancel, they will be redirected to the redirect URI with and `error` query param added. L233: L234: `www.example.com/my-redirect-uri?error=access_denied&state= L235: ` L236: You can use this `error`query parameter to conditionally update your app’s state as needed. If the user opts to `Select pages`, then a page picker interface opens. A user can search for and select pages and databases to share with the connection from the page picker. L237: L238: The page picker only displays pages or databases to which a user has 【60†full access†www.notion.com】, because a user needs full access to a resource in order to be able to share it with a connection. L239: 【61†Image: Checkboxes let the user choose which pages to share.†mintcdn.com】 L240: L241: Page picker interface L242: Users can select which pages to give the connection access to, including both private and public pages available to them. Parent pages can be selected to quickly provide access to child pages, as giving access to a parent page will provide access to all available child pages. Users can return to this view at a later time to update access settings if circumstances change. If the user clicks `Allow access`, they are then redirected to the `redirect_uri` with a temporary authorization `code`. L243: If the user denies access, they are redirected to the `redirect_uri` with an `error` query parameter. If the user clicks `Allow access` and the rest of the auth flow is not completed, the connection will not have access to the pages that were selected. L244: #### Prompt for a connection with a Notion template option L245: L246: OAuth integrations offer the option of providing a public Notion page to use as a template during the auth flow. L69: ### OAuth【39†⁠】 L70: L71: If you’re building an application for others to use, we recommend you use 【12†OAuth2 authentication】. Once you complete the authentication flow and acquire an access token, pass it with the header `Authorization: Bearer ` L72: L73: `curl \ L74: -X POST \ L75: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ L76: -H "Authorization: Bearer " \ L77: --data '{ "query": "{ issues { nodes { id title } } }" }' \ L78: https://api.linear.app/graphql` L79: ### Personal API Keys【40†⁠】 L80: L81: For personal scripts API keys are the easiest way to access the API. L82: L83: To authenticate your requests, you need to pass the API key with header: `Authorization: ` L84: L85: `curl \ L86: -X POST \ L87: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ L88: -H "Authorization: " \ L89: --data '{ "query": "{ issues { nodes { id title } } }" }' \ L90: https://api.linear.app/graphql` L91: ## Error handling【42†⁠】 L92: L93: Linear’s GraphQL API follows the standard GraphQL error format, returning errors within an errors array in the response. Each error object includes a message describing what went wrong, a path array indicating where in the query the L94: error occurred, and extensions that may contain additional context such as error codes or validation details. L95: Always check for the errors array before assuming success—GraphQL queries can partially succeed with a 200 HTTP status, returning some data while L96: including errors for failed fields. Monitor HTTP status codes for server errors (5xx) and make sure to correctly handle 【6†rate limits】. Use strongly-typed GraphQL clients when possible to catch validation errors at development time, and always validate required fields to avoid runtime null value errors. L107: ### Queries & Mutations【46†⁠】 L108: L109: To get information about the authenticated user, you can use the `viewer` query: L110: L111: `query Me { L112: viewer { L113: id L114: name L115: email L116: } L117: }` L118: L119: As issues (and most other objects) are team based, you first need to get the ID of the team you want to interact with: L120: L121: `query Teams { L122: teams { L123: nodes { L124: id L125: name L126: } L127: } L128: }` L129: Once you have found the correct team, you can get the issues for that team. L162: ### Creating & Editing Issues【47†⁠】 L163: L164: To create a new issue, use a mutation: L165: L166: `mutation IssueCreate { L167: issueCreate( L168: input: { L169: title: "New exception" L170: description: "More detailed error report in markdown" L171: teamId: "9cfb482a-81e3-4154-b5b9-2c805e70a02d" L172: } L173: ) { L174: success L175: issue { L176: id L177: title L178: } L179: } L180: }` L181: This mutation will create a new issue and return its `id` and `title` if the call was successful (`success: true`). L182: L183: If an issue is created without a specified `stateId`(the status field for the issue), the issue will be assigned to the team’s first state in the Backlog workflow state category. If the “Triage” feature is turned on for the team, then the issue will be assigned to the Triage workflow state. L184: A common use case after creating an issue is updating the issue. To do this we can use the `issueUpdate` mutation, using the input field to include whatever it is we want to change. The `id` provided can be either be the uuid returned by the creation query, or the shorthand id like `BLA-123` below. L185: L186: `mutation IssueUpdate { L187: issueUpdate( L188: id: "BLA-123", L189: input: { L190: title: "New Issue Title" L191: stateId: "NEW-STATE-ID", L192: } L193: ) { L194: success L195: issue { L196: id L197: title L198: state { L199: id L200: name L201: } L202: } L203: } L204: }` L205: Changes made to an issue’s properties in the first 3 minutes are considered part of the issue creation process, and won’t be added to the activity log as changes to the issue. L206: ### Accessing Images【48†⁠】 L207: L208: Linear hosts images and other assets uploaded into Linear behind authentication. Only authenticated users can view their assets. This also applies to the API and all images will require authentication to be displayed outside Linear’s application. Regular 【38†API authentication】 (OAuth or API keys) is accepted for displaying images. If you’re displaying images outside Linear’s applications, you should download and self-host them in your application’s environment. L209: ### Adding mentions in Markdown【49†⁠】 L210: L211: In the Linear application, you can add mentions to users, issues, projects, and other resources by typing @ and then selecting a resource to mention. L212: L213: In the GraphQL API, mentions can be created in Markdown by using the plain URL of the resource. L222: ### Adding collapsible sections in Markdown【50†⁠】 L223: L224: For collapsible sections in an issue, comment, or document, use `+++ [some section title]` to start the section and `+++` to end it. L225: L226: `+++ Section title L227: L228: Markdown content (initially hidden) L229: L230: +++` L231: ### Fetching Updates【51†⁠】 L232: L233: If you’re working on building an application which displays Linear data and you want the information to update (near) realtime, you have few options. L234: L235: Lets say you’re displaying a big number of issues in your application and want to update them: L236: L237: Do: L238: * Register 【8†a programmatic webhook】 and get updates for all issues for the team. integrations L123: L124: Integrations with Jira Cloud can be implemented by allowing external applications or services, scripts, or even bots, to access Jira's APIs directly. If you are not doing this and you are using the Connect framework instead, see 【36†Security for Connect apps】. L125: Authentication and authorization are the two key parts of implementing security. Authentication tells Jira Cloud the identity of your integration, and authorization determines what actions it can take within Jira. If you are building an integration that does not use Atlassian Connect, there are two methods that you can use for authentication and authorization: L126: * OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO): This is the recommended method. You should use this for most cases. L127: * Basic authentication: You should only use this method for tools like personal scripts or bots. L128: ## OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO) L129: L130: OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants, also known as three-legged OAuth, is a token-based method for authentication and authorization. This method allows your integration to access Atlassian product APIs on a user's behalf. Unlike two-legged OAuth, three-legged OAuth involves the end user in the authorization process by asking them to consent to access to their data. L131: Authenticated access is provided by an access token that is used to make calls to the API. OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants require an app created in the 【37†developer console】. This app provides the authentication credentials that are used to get an access token for the desired API. L132: Authorization for OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants is implemented via scopes. Scopes statically specify the maximum set of actions that an app may perform (see 【38†scopes】). Note, OAuth 2.0 authorization code-only scopes are different to 【39†Connect scopes】. L133: L134: To learn more, read 【40†OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO)】. L135: ## Basic authentication L136: L137: Basic authentication uses an API token to authenticate the client. The token is generated from a user's Atlassian Account, encoded, then added to the header for requests to the API. L138: L139: Authorization for basic authentication is based on the permissions of the user you used to generate the API token. For example, if you are using basic authentication, your user must have the Edit Issue permission on an issue in order to make a PUT request to the `/issue` resource. L140: We recommend that you don't use basic authentication. It may be easier to implement, but it is much less secure. Consider using OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO) instead. L141: L142: To learn more, read 【41†Basic auth for REST APIs】. The purpose of your app, who uses it, and its features will dictate the method of auth that’s best for your app. Here are the various authentication options and why you might want to use each of them. L27: L28: * * * L29: ## L30: L31: Personal access token L32: L33: A 【10†personal access token】 (PAT) is the quickest and simplest way to authenticate in the API. PATs are long-lived tokens allowing programmatic authentication to the API and should be stored securely. PATs provide the same authorization (i.e., permissions and level of access to Asana data) through the API as the user who generated them has in the Asana web product. L34: Using a PAT is a good way to get started quickly with the API regardless of which auth type you end up using in production. If you are building a script or simple app that doesn’t need to support multiple users logging in, then using a PAT with your production app is a sufficient option. L35: If your app needs more access to data than you have in Asana, then you should consider using a 【11†Service Account†help.asana.com】. You will likely want to use 【12†OAuth】 if your app needs to support multiple users signing in to use the app. L36: L37: PATs are generated in the 【7†developer console†app.asana.com】. See the 【10†PAT documentation】 for more information. L38: ### L39: L40: PAT attribution L41: L42: If you generate a PAT from your Asana account, any API actions that are authenticated with your PAT will be attributed to you in the Asana web product. For example, if a script uses your PAT to authenticate an API request to comment on a task, the comment will appear to be made by you in the Asana app. L43: If you prefer against having your app’s actions to be authored by you, then you should provision a new Asana user (or guest account) and then generate the PAT from this new account. This user will act as a "bot" account. You should give the account a name and photo that will make it clear to Asana users that an app is taking action and not a person. More details on this approach can be found in the 【13†Bots and scopes】 section of this guide. L44: L45: * * * L46: ## L47: L48: Service Account L49: L50: Similar to PATs, 【11†Service Accounts†help.asana.com】 (SAs) are long-lived tokens that provide programmatic access to the API. Service Accounts are an 【14†Enterprise tier†asana.com】 feature and can only be created by Asana super admins (see more about 【15†admin roles at Asana†help.asana.com】). L51: Unlike PATs, SAs provide complete access to all data within your Asana account, including private user data. As such, SAs are ideal if your app needs to have org-wide authorization. Some common use cases include: L52: * Creating periodic data backups L53: * Automating programmatic management of your Asana account. For example: L54: * User management and access based on company's policies L55: * Administrative tasks like team member management L56: * Cleaning up inactive projects L57: * Standardizing the structure of objects in your domain (e.g., portfolios, projects, custom fields, etc.) L58: * Building integrations that require access to all Asana data L59: * Authenticating Asana API endpoints that require service accounts. For example: L60: * 【16†Audit log】 L61: * 【17†Organizational exports】 L62: * 【18†SCIM】 L63: Instructions for Asana super admins to generate Service Accounts: L64: L65: 1. Click the Apps tab from within the admin console L66: 2. Click Service Accounts L67: 3. Click the Add Service Account button L68: L69: > 📘 L70: > L71: > ### L72: > L73: > Service Account Scopes L74: > L75: > To learn more about how Service Account scopes and how to configure them for your specific use case – check out our 【19†Service Account Scopes documentation】 L76: L77: * * * L78: ## L79: L80: OAuth L81: L82: OAuth is an open-standard authentication protocol that allows you to approve one application interacting with another on your behalf without providing your username and password. This is the best choice if multiple users need to sign in to your app. L83: L84: OAuth is more complex to implement than using token-based auth (i.e., PATs and SAs), but it offers more features and security. To implement OAuth, follow the detailed instructions in our 【12†OAuth documentation】. L85: L86: * * * L87: ## L88: L89: OpenID Connect L90: L91: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an open authentication protocol that works on top of the OAuth 2.0. The purpose of OIDC is for users to provide one set of credentials and access multiple sites. L92: L93: If you want to allow users to log into your app using their Asana account, the OpenID Connect protocol is a great way to have your apps users authenticate. L94: L95: See the 【20†OpenID Connect documentation】 for more information. L19: ## Personal access tokens L20: L21: The API can be accessed by creating a Personal Access Token from the 【6†Developers†id.getharvest.com】 section of Harvest ID. L22: Personal Access Tokens are the preferred method when you want to write your own scripts that consume our API. L23: Personal Access Tokens replace the Basic Authentication method that was used in our v1 API, as this is more secure. L24: Once generated, a Personal Access Token can be used to access the API by either providing the token in the Authorization header or including it in the query string. L82: L83: ### L84: L85: Is it possible to get pending transactions via the API? L86: L87: This is not available through the API today. L88: ### L89: L90: Can you filter transactions using a time range through the API? L91: L92: This is not available through the API today, but the current workaround is to 【28†request all transactions】 and then filter the transactions on your side. L93: L94: ### L95: L96: Is there a way to check the balance of a user's deposit account using the API? L97: L98: Yes, the 【26†List Cash Accounts endpoint】 returns the current balance of each account. L99: ### L100: L101: How do I get a card's PAN? L102: L103: You can use the 【29†Get Card Number endpoint】 to get a card's PAN. L110: ### L111: L112: How do I get the request trace ID to help with support requests? L113: L114: It is in the API response header called `X-Brex-Trace-Id`. A principal is who you are (your identity), and a token is how you prove it (your credential). Understanding this distinction is the key to choosing the right authentication method for your use case. L185: ## Principals & tokens L186: L187: Principal | Token | Description L188: --- | --- | --- L189: Service User (non-human) | Service User API Key | For automated integrations and CI/CD pipelines L190: User (human) | Personal Access Token (PAT) | For human programmatic access under your own identity L191: All API credentials use the `cog_` prefix format. Include your token in the `Authorization` header of every request: L192: L193: `curl -X GET "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \ L194: -H "Authorization: Bearer cog_your_token_here" L195: ` L196: L197: The key distinction is which principal the token authenticates as: L198: * A Service User API Key authenticates as the service user — the service user’s identity, permissions, and org memberships apply. L199: * A Personal Access Token authenticates as the human user who created it — that user’s identity, permissions, and org memberships apply. L200: ### Personal access token or service user? L201: | Personal access token | Service user API key L202: --- | --- | --- L203: Acts as | You | A separate non-human identity L204: Permissions | Exactly yours, in every organization you have access to | The role you give the service user, in the organizations it is added to L205: Scope | Your account. Each request names the organization | Created at the organization or enterprise level L206: Audit trail | Attributed to you | Attributed to the service user, even when it creates a session on someone’s behalf with `create_as_user_id` L207: Lifecycle | Tied to you. Revoked automatically if you leave the account | Not tied to any person, so it survives team changes L208: Best for | Personal scripts, local tooling, the Devin CLI and desktop apps | CI/CD, production integrations, shared automation L209: Rule of thumb: if the integration should keep working after you leave the team or change roles, use a service user. If it should do exactly what you can do, as you, use a PAT. L210: L211: * * * L212: ## Service users (recommended for automation) L213: L214: Service users are non-human accounts designed for API integrations. They can be assigned specific permissions via RBAC and added to organizations independently of human users. L215: ### How it works L216: 1. Provision a service user in Settings > Devin API (Service users tab) for an organization, or Enterprise settings > Devin API (Service users tab) for the enterprise L217: 2. Assign a role that controls which endpoints the service user can access. You pick a role from a dropdown, not individual permissions L218: 3. Choose an expiration — it defaults to 30 days; the other options are 7 days, 90 days, and, where your account allows it, Never L219: 4. Copy the API key — the key starts with `cog_` and is shown only once, right after provisioning L220: 5. Use the key in the `Authorization` header of every API request L221: L222: `curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/$DEVIN_ORG_ID/sessions" \ L223: -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY" \ L224: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ L225: -d '{"prompt": "Create a simple Python script"}' L226: ` L227: ### Service user scopes L228: L229: Scope | Created in | API access | Use case L230: --- | --- | --- | --- L231: Organization | Settings > Devin API > Service users | `/v3/organizations/*` | Session management, knowledge, playbooks, secrets L232: Enterprise | Enterprise settings > Devin API > Service users | `/v3/enterprise/*` + `/v3/organizations/*` | Cross-org management, analytics, audit logs, billing L233: L234: Find your organization ID at the top of the Settings > Devin API page. L235: ### Session attribution with `create_as_user_id` L236: L237: Service users are separate identities from human users. By default, sessions created by a service user are attributed to the service user itself. To create sessions on behalf of a specific user, pass the `create_as_user_id` parameter when creating a session. The session will appear in that user’s session list and count toward their usage. This requires the `ImpersonateOrgSessions` permission on the service user’s role. L245: L246: * * * L247: ## Personal access tokens L248: Personal Access Tokens (PATs) allow human users to authenticate programmatically under their own identity. When you use a PAT, the API sees you — your permissions, your org memberships, and your audit trail. This is useful when you want to make API calls as yourself (e.g., personal scripts, local tooling) rather than through a shared service user. A PAT is not scoped to an organization or an enterprise. It belongs to you within your account and works in every organization you have access to. # How to Test a Webhook (Troubleshooting Guide)

Edited Friday, October 2 2026

This guide will help you test whether your endpoint can successfully receive webhooks from Fathom. It includes some initial configuration checks and explains how to send a test webhook from your API key configuration page.

Note: For more information about creating and configuring webhooks, see the Fathom API documentation.

## Initial Checks (Before Testing)

Please confirm the following:

  1. Your endpoint is configured as a POST endpoint

     * Not GET

  2. You're using the Production URL

     * Not a Test URL

  3. If using n8n:

     * Use the Production URL, not the Test URL.

     * Confirm that the workflow toggle is green and displays Active.

  4. Confirm that the webhook URL shown in Fathom matches the intended destination.

## Send a Test Webhook from Fathom

  1. In Fathom, open User Settings → API Access.

  2. Open the API key configuration page associated with your webhook.

  3. Click Send Test Payload.

Fathom will send a test webhook to the configured destination using an example payload from one of your meetings.

## Understanding the Test Result

If your endpoint returns a successful `2xx` response, such as `200` or `202`, it confirms that:

  * The endpoint received the request

  * The server accepted it

A successful response does not necessarily confirm that:

  * Every value was processed as expected

  * Your downstream logic executed successfully

  * The full workflow completed successfully

After sending the test, check your endpoint or workflow’s execution history to confirm that the payload was processed correctly.

If Fathom successfully sends the test but the downstream workflow does not complete, review the receiving platform’s logs and configuration or contact that platform’s support team for assistance. Fathom Support can help confirm Fathom’s webhook configuration and delivery but does not configure or debug third-party workflows.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Generate an API token

To use the API, you’ll first need an API token. You create and manage your tokens in your Superhuman Docs account settings. A token is tied to your account, so it can never do more than you can in Docs.

## Create a token

  1. Go to docs.superhuman.com/account

  2. Scroll down to the API connections section

  3. Click the Generate API token button

  4. Give your token a name

  5. Choose a permission level: Read only (the default), Write only, or Read and write. Your choice applies to every resource you select below.

  6. Choose what your token can access. All content is selected by default. This will grant access to all docs and their content.

    1. You can narrow the accessible content by choosing Selected content. Then select up to 10 docs or tables.

    2. Add other resources, such as Packs, the Docs MCP, or your organization (Enterprise org admins only)

  7. Click Generate API token to confirm

  8. Your new token will appear at the top of the list. Click the Copy token button to copy and use.

Image: create API token (no restrictions).gif

Tip: Choose the most restrictive access that meets your needs. If your integration only needs to read data from your docs, keep the default Read only permission.

## Understand token access

  * A default token can read, but not write. It can read your docs, but it can’t make changes, and it has no access to Packs, your organization, or the MCP.

  * Read + write is a deliberate choice. To let a token make changes, switch the permission level to Read and write when you create it.

  * One permission level per token. The permission level applies to all of the resources you select. If you need different permission levels for different resources, create separate tokens.

  * A token can’t exceed your own access. Your token can only access what your account can access, and your organization’s policies still apply.

  * The MCP is opt-in. The MCP is only included if you select it. Note that choosing specific docs limits what the token can do through the API only. It doesn’t restrict the MCP to those docs. To learn more, see Control what the Docs MCP can access.

## Token expiration

Note: This section applies only to members of a Docs Enterprise org. Enterprise org admins can view all of the API tokens in their org, set the org’s token expiration limit, and revoke tokens via admin settings. If you’re an org admin, you can learn more here.

Org admins can set an expiration limit for API tokens across their org. If your org has a limit, your tokens will expire after that period, and the expiration date will show next to each token in your API connections list.

Image: user account API connections - expiration date.png

When a token is about to expire, you’ll get an email notification starting 14 days before the expiration date, with reminder emails after that. Once a token expires, any apps, scripts, or services using it will lose access to the API.

You can refresh an expiring token by following the steps below. Note that once the token expires, it cannot be refreshed - you will need to create a new token instead.

  1. Click the link in the notification email, or go to docs.superhuman.com/account and scroll to API connections

  2. Click the three-dot menu, and select Refresh token

  3. Copy the new token, then update your apps and scripts to use it. Note: The old token value stops working as soon as you refresh.

Your token keeps its place in the list, with an updated creation date and expiration date. Each token also shows a status: Active, Expiring soon (14 days or fewer until it expires), or Expired.

If you no longer need a token, you don’t need to regenerate it. You can ignore the email, or delete the token from your API connections list (three-dot menu > Revoke).

# FAQs

Are there API size limits on requests?

The limit for requests is 2 MB, but there is also a limit of 85 KB for any given row. See this community post for more details.

Are API limits per workspace, user, or token?

Limits are attached to a user/IP.

Why can’t my token make changes to my docs?

If you’re unable to make edits to your docs via your API token, this could be because the API token is limited to only certain docs or because the token is read-only. You can check the token details in the API connections section of your account settings and, if needed, create a new, more permissive token.

Why am I getting a 429 rate limit error?

If you’re getting a 429 error when trying to use Superhuman Docs’ API, you are running into the API rate limit. Superhuman Docs sets a limit on the number of requests that can be made per minute. For the latest info on the specific rate limits, check out this resource.

The API is returning a date and time stamp different than I’d expect. Why is that?

The API returns dates in Pacific time. The user can write code to offset from there.

How do I send an image to the API?

Coda will ask for your API token in order to connect to the Jira Pack. In Jira, this is called the Personal Access Token. You can find this in Jira following these steps:

  2. Select Personal Access Token in the left-hand menu

  4. Give your new token a name
